passages.name: Marigold
passages.head: The fyrste boke of the vertues of certayne Herbes
passages.text: The firste herbe is called with the men of Chaldea, Elios with the Grekes, Matuchiol, with the Latynes, Elitropium, with English men, Marygolde, whose interpretation, is of Elios, that is the Sonne, and Tropos, that is alteration, or chaunge, because it is turned according to … sunne The vertue of this herbe is maruelous: for if it be gathered, the Sunne beyng in the signe Leo, in August, and be wrapped in the leafe of a Laurell, or baye tree, & a wolues to the be added therto, no mam shalbe able to haue a word to speake against the bearer therof, but woordes of peace. And yf any thing be stolen, if the bearer of the thinges before named, lay them vnder hys head in the nyght, he shall see the thefe, & all hys com ditions. And moreouer, yt the forsayd herbe be put in any church, where women be, whyche haue broken Matrymonye on theyr parte, they shall neuer be able to go forthe of the churche, excepte it be put awaye. And thys last poynte hath bene proued, and is very true.

passages.name: Nettle
passages.head: The fyrste boke of the vertues of certayne Herbes
passages.text: The seconde herbe is called of the men of Chaldea Roybra, of … Grekes Olieribus, of the Latynes, or Frenchemen Vrtica, of English men, a nettell. He that holsteth this herbe in hys hande, with an herbe called Mylfoyle, or yarowe, or noseblede, is sure from all feare, & fantasye, or vysion. And yf it be put with the iuyce of houselyke, and the bearers hande be anoynted with it, and the residue be put in water, if he entre in the water where fysshes be, they wil gather together to hys handes, and also ad piscellum. And if hys hande be drawem forth, they will leape agayne to theyr owne places, where they were before.

passages.name: Celandine
passages.head: The fyrste boke of the vertues of certayne Herbes
passages.text: The fourthe hearbe, is named Aquilaris, of Chaldeis: because it springeth in the time, in whiche the Egles buylde their nestes: It is named of Grekes Ualis, of La tines Celidonia, and of Englishmen Celendyne. This hearbe springeth in the time, in that which the swallo wes, and also the Egles maketh their nestes. If any man shal haue this herbe, with the hart of a molle, he shall ouercome all his enemies, and all matters in suit, & shall put a waie all debate. And if the before named hearbe, be put vpon the headde of a sycke man, if he should dye, he shal sing anone with a loude boyce, if not, he shall wepe.

passages.name: Hound's tongue
passages.head: The fyrste boke of the vertues of certayne Herbes
passages.text: The seuenthe herbe is named of the Chaldeis Algeil, of the Grekes Drum, of the Latins Lingua canis, of English men, Hondes tounge, put thou this herbe with the hart of a yonge frogge, & her matrice, and put them where thou wilte, and a fter a littel tyme, all the dogges of the whole town shalbe gathered together: And if thou shalte haue the afore named herbe vnder thy formest toe, al the dogges shall kepe silence, & shal not haue power to bark.

passages.name: Lily
passages.head: The fyrste boke of the vertues of certayne Herbes
passages.text: The nynth herbe, is named of the Chaldeis Ango, of the Greekes Amala, of the Latines Lilium, of the English men a Lyly. If thou wilt gather this herbe, the sonne beyng in the signe of the Lyon, & wilt myxe it with the iuyce of the Laurel, or baye tree, & afterward thou shalt put that iuyce vnder the dunge of cattell, a certayn tyme, it shalbe turned vnto wormes, of the whiche, if poulder be made, & be put about the necke of ani mam or in hys clothes, he shall neuer slepe, nor shal not be able to slepe vntyll it be put a waye. And yf thou shalt put the aforesaide thing vnder the dunge of cattel, and wilt anoynte any man with the wormes bredinge thereof, he shalbe brought anon vnto a fenex. And yf the aforesayd thynge be put in any vessel, where there is comes mylke, and be couered with the skynne of anye cowe of one collour, all the kye shall loose their mylke.

passages.name: Mistletoe
passages.head: The fyrste boke of the vertues of certayne Herbes
passages.text: The tenth herbe is called of the Chaldeis Luperax, of the Grekes A…ifena, of the Latines Uiscus querci, of Englishe men Myssell toe. And it groweth in trees, beynge holed through. This herbe with a certaim other herbe, which is named Martegon, that is Silphion or Laserpitium, as it is written in the Almaynes language, it openeth all lockes. And if the aforesayde thinges, being put together, be put in the mouthe of anye man, yf he thynke of anye thyng, yf it shoulde happen, it is set on hys harte, yf not, it lepeth backe from his hart. If the afore sayd thyng be hanged vp to a tree with the wyng of a swallow, there the brydes shalbe gathered together wrihin the space of fyue myles. And this laste was proued in my tyme.

passages.name: Centaury
passages.head: The fyrste boke of the vertues of certayne Herbes
passages.text: The eleuenth herbe is named of the Chaldeis Isiphilon, of the Grekes Orgelon, of the Latines Centaurea, of English men Centory, which sayth that ths herbe hath a marualous vertue, for yf it be ioyned with the bloude of a female lapwyng, or black plouer and be put with oyle in a lampe, all they that compasse it aboute, shal beleue them selfes to be witches, so that one shal beleue of an other, that his head is in heauen and his fete in the earth. And yf the aforefayd thing be put in the fyre wham the starres shyne it shall appeare, that the starres runne one agaynst an other, and fight. And if the aforesayde playster be put to the nosethrilles of any mam, he shall flee away sharpely, through feare that he shall haue, & thys hath ben proude.

passages.name: Sage
passages.head: The fyrste boke of the vertues of certayne Herbes
passages.text: The twelft herbe is named of the Chaldeis Colorio, or Coloricon, of the Grekes Clamor, of the Latines commonlye Saluia, of Englysh mem Sauge. Thys herbe beyng putrified vnder dunge of cattell, in a glasyn vessell, bryngeth forthe a certayne worme or byrd, hauyng a tayle after the fasshion of the byrde, called a blacke macke or owsyll, with whose bloud, yf any man be touched in the brest, he shall lose hys sence or felynge the space of.xv. dayes and more. And yf the aforesaid Serpent be burned, & the asshes of it put in the fyre, anone shall there be a rayne bowe, with an horrible thunder. And yf the aforesayde asshes be put in a lampe, and be kyndled, it shall appeare that al the house is ful of serpentes, & thys hath ben proued of men of late tyme.

passages.name: Vervain
passages.head: The fyrste boke of the vertues of certayne Herbes
passages.text: The.xiii. herbe, is named of the Chaldeis Olphanas, of the Grekes Hiliorion, of the Latines Verbena of the English mem Veruyn. This herbe (as witches say) gathered, the Sunne beyng in the signe of the Ram, & put with grayne or corne of pyonie of one yeare olde healeth them the be sicke of the fallyng sykenes. And if it be put in a fatte ground, after.viii. wekes wormes shalbe engendred, which yf they shall touche any man, he shall dye anone. And if the aforesayd thing be put in a doue house or a culuer house, al the doues or culuers shalbe gathered together there. And if the poulder of them be put in the sunne, it shal appeare that the sunne is blue. If the poulder be put in a place where men dwell or lye betwen two louers, anone there is made stryfe or malyce betwene them.

passages.name: Smallage
passages.head: The fyrste boke of the vertues of certayne Herbes
passages.text: The.xiiii. herbe is named of the Chaldeis Celayos, of the Greekes Casini. of the Latines Melisopholos, of English men Smalage: of the which herbe Macer floridus maketh mention. This herbe gathered grene, and tasten with the iuyce of the Cypresse tree of one yeare, put in gruell, maketh the gruell to appere full of wormes, and maketh the bearer to be gentle & gratious, & to vanquish his aduersaries. And yf the aforesayde herbe be bounden to an oxes neck, he wil folow the whether soeuer thou wilte goo.

passages.name: Rose
passages.head: The fyrste boke of the vertues of certayne Herbes
passages.text: The.xv. herbe is named of the Chaldeis Glerisa, of the Grekes Isaphinus, of the Latines Rosa, of English mem a Rose. And it is an herbe, whose floure is verye well knowell. Take the grain or corne of it, & the corne of musterd seede and the foote of a Wesel, hanged vp these in a tree, and it will not beare fruyte after. And yf the aforesayde thinge be put aboute a nette, fysshes will gather together there. And if Magaris shall be dead & be put in the aforesayd commixtion halfe a daye, it shall recouer the lyfe, althoughe it be not forth with yet gotten.

passages.name: Snake's grass
passages.head: The fyrste boke of the vertues of certayne Herbes
passages.text: The.xvi. herbe is called of the Chaldeis Carturlin, of the Grekes Pentaphyllon, of the Latynes Serpentina, in English snakes grasse. Thys herbe is well ynough knowen with vs. Thys herbe put in the grounde, wyth the leafe of the thre leafed grasse engendreth read & grene serpentes, of which if poulder be made, and put in a burnynge lampe, there shall appeare aboundaunce of serpentes. And if it be put vnder the head of ani man, from thence forth he shall not dreame of hym selfe.

passages.name: Lodestone
passages.head: If thou wilt knowe whyther thy wyfe is chaste, or no
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Magnes in English, the lode stone, it is of sadde bl…w coloure, and it is founde in the sea of Inde sometime in partes of Almaine, in the prouince, which is called East Fraunce. Laye thys stone vnder the head of a wyfe, & yf she be chast, she wil embrace her husbande, if she be not chaste, she wil fall anone forth of the bedde.

passages.name: Ophthalmius
passages.head: If thou wilt knowe whyther thy wyfe is chaste, or no
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Ophethalmius, and wrappe it in the leafe of the Laurell, or Baye tree, & it is called Lapis obtelmicus, whose colour is not named, …or it is of many colours, and it is of such vertu, that it blindeth the sightes of them that stand about. Constantinus carying this in hys hande, was made inuisyble by it.
passages.title: If thou wilt be made inuisible

passages.name: Onyx
passages.head: If thou wilt prouoke sorowe, feare, terrible fantasyes, & debate
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Onyz, which is of black coloure. And the kynd is best which is ful of whyte vaynes. And it commeth from Inde, vnto Araby, and if it be hanged vpon the necke, or fynger, it styrreth vp anone sorowe or heauynesse in a man, and terroures, and also debate, and this hath bene proued by men of late tyme.

passages.name: Fire stone
passages.head: If thou wilt burne any mans handes without fyre
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Fet…pendamus, which is of yelow colour, which if it be hanged vpom the necke of anye man, it healeth Areticum, and also if this stone be greped straytly, it burneth the hand anone, & therfore it must be touched lightly, and gently.

passages.name: Selenite
passages.head: If thou wilt kyndle the mynd of any man too ioyes, and make hys wytte sharpe
passages.text: Take the stone, whiche is called Sylonites, & it groweth in the bosome of a snayle of Inde, called Corcuses, and there is of dyuers kyndes of it, of whyte, read, and purple colour. Other saye, that it is grene, and found in the partes of Parsia. And also olde Philosophers saye, if it be tasted, it geueth knowledge of certayne thinges to come. If it be put vnder the tounge, specially in the first mone, it hath a vertue onely for an houre. Therfore beyng in the x. moone, it hath thys vertue in the fyrst, or tenth houre. But there is mouyng of the order, because, whan it is vnder the tung, if our thought be of any busynes, whether it oughte too be or no, if it oughte to be, it is fixed stedfastlye to the hart, so that it may not be plucked awaye, if not, the harte leapeth abacke from it. Also Philosophers haue sayd, that it healeth Ptificos, and weake men.

passages.name: Topaz
passages.head: If thou wilt that seething water come furth anone, after thou hast put in thy hand
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Topazion, fro the Ile Topasis, or because it shesheth a similitude of golde. And there be twoo kyndes of it: one is vtterlye lyke golde, and thys is more precious The other kynde is of the colour of saffron, of bryghter colour tham golde is, and thys is more profitable. It hath ben proued in oure time, that if it be put in seething water. it maketh it to runne ouer but if thou put thy. hande in it, the water is drawen out anone, and one of our brethren did thys at Paryse. It is good also agaynste Emothoicam et stimaticam, or lunatyke, passion or griefe.

passages.name: Medora
passages.head: If thou wilt pluck of the skynne of thyne, or an other mans hande
passages.text: Take the stone, whiche is called Medora, of the region Media in the which the people dwelling are called Medi. And there bee two kyndes of it, blacke & grene. It is sayde of olde Philosophers and also of Phylosophers, beyng in thys tyme, if the blacke be broken, and resolued in hote water, if any man wathe hys handes in that water, the skynne of his ham des shalbe plucked of anone.

passages.name: Asbestos
passages.head: If thou wilt make a fyre continually vnable to be quem shed or put out
passages.text: Take the stone, whiche is called Abaston, & it is of the colour of yron; and there is founde very muche of it in Arabia. If that stoone be kyndeled or inflamed, it maye neuer bee putte oute, or quenched, because it hath the nature of the fyrst fethers of the Salamandre, by reason of moystye fatnesse, which nourissheth the fyre, kyndled in it.

passages.name: Diamond
passages.head: If thou wilte ouercome thy enemyes
passages.text: Take the stone, whiche is called Adamas, in English speache, a Diamonde, and it is of shyning colour, & very harde, in so muche that it can not be broken, but by the bloud of a gote, & it groweth in Arabia, or in Cypres. And if it be bounden to the lefte side, it is good agaynst enemies, madnes, wyld beastes, venomouse beastes and cruell men, and agaynst chydyng & brawlynge. & agaynst venyme, and inuaston of fantasyes, and some call it Diamas.

passages.name: Agate
passages.head: If thou wilt eschew all peri… and all terrible thinges, & haue a stronge harte
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Agathes, & it is blacke, and hath whyte vaynes. There is another of the same kynde, lyke to whyte colour. And the thyrde groweth in a certayn Ile, hauynge blacke vaynes, & that maketh too ouercome peryls, & geue strength to the hart. & maketh a man mightye, pleasaunte, delectable, & helpeth agaynst aduersities.

passages.name: Esmundus
passages.head: If thou wilt ouercome beastes and interprete, or expounde all dreames and prophe cye of thynges to come
passages.text: Take the stone, whiche is called Esmundus or Asmadus, it is of diuers colours, it putteth out all poyson, and maketh a man to ouercome hys aduersaries, & geueth Prophesieng, and the interpretation of all dreames, & maketh a man to vnderstande darke questions, harde to be vnderstand or assoyled.

passages.name: Amethyst
passages.head: If thou wilt haue good vnder standing of thynges that may be felte, and that thou maye not be made dronked
passages.text: Take the stone, whithe is called Amaristus, and it is of purple colour, and the beste is founde in Inde, and it is good agaynst drum kennes, and geueth good vnderstandynge in thynges that maye be vnderstande.

passages.name: Beryl
passages.head: If thou wilt ouercom thy enemyes, and slee debate
passages.text: Take the stone, whiche is called Berillus, it is of pale coloure and may be sene through as water, bear it about with thee, and thou shalt ouercome all debate, & shalte dryue a waye thy enemies and it maketh thy enemye meke. It causeth a manne too be well manuered, as Aaron sayethe, it geueth also good vnderstandinge.

passages.name: Celonites
passages.head: If thou wilt foreiudge, or coniecture of thynges to come
passages.text: Take the stone, whiche is called Celonites, it is of purple, & diuerse other colours, & it is founde in the head of the snayle. If any man will beare thys stone vnder hys tunge, he shal foreiudge, and propheci of thinges to come. But notwithstanding, it hath no vertue, but shynynge, Prima cunfuerit accensa, et crescens monoytes in vltima descendente, soo meaneth Aaron, in the boke of vertues of herbes, and stones.

passages.name: Coral
passages.head: If thou wilt pacifie tempestes and go ouer fluddes
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Corallus, Corall, & some be read and some whyte. And it hath ben proueth that it stemmeth anone bloude, and putteth away the folishnes of hym that beareth it, & geueth wysedom. And this hath ben proued of certayn mem in our tyme. And it is good agaynst tempestes, and perils of fluddes.

passages.name: Crystal
passages.head: If thou wilt kendle fyre
passages.text: Take the Christal stone, & put it nygh vnder the cirkle of the Sum ne, that is to sai, against the sunne and put it nygh any thing that may be burned, & incontinently, the heat of the Sunne shyning, will set it a fyre.

passages.name: Bloodstone
passages.head: If thou wilt that the Sunne appeare of bloudy colour
passages.text: Take the stone, whiche is called Elitropia. It is grene like to the precious stone called the Emeraude. And it is sprynkled wyth bloudy droppes. The necromancers call it Gemma Babylonica, the precious stone of Babylom, by the propre name. But if it be anoynted with the iuyce of an her be of the same name, and be put in a vesselful of water, it maketh the Sunne to seme of bloudy colour: as if the Eclypse were sene. The caus of this is, for it maketh al the water to bubble vp vnto a little cloude, which makyng the ayre thycke: letteth the Sunne to be sene, but as it were read, in a thicke color, a little after: the cloud goeth away, by droppyng doune lyke dew, as it were by droppes of rayne. Thys also borne about maketh a mam of good fame, hole: and of longe lyfe.

passages.name: Epibretes
passages.head: If thou wilt make sething water too be colde, whiche standeth vpon the fyre
passages.text: Take the stone, whych is called Epibretes, which put in water agaynst the eye of the Sunne, putteth forth fyery beames of the Sunne. And it is sayd of olde, and new Philosophers, if it be put in seethyng water, the bublyng vp, or seethyng will sone cease, and a litle after, it will waxe colde. and it is a shynynge and ruddye stoone.

passages.name: Chalcedony
passages.head: If thou wilt eschewe illusions and fantasies & ouercome all causes or matters
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Calcedonius, & it is pale, brown of coloure, & somewhat darke, yf thys be perced, & hanged about the necke, with the stone which is called Sinerip, it is good against al fantastical illusions, & it maketh to ouercome all causes, or matters in suyte, & kepeth thy bodye agaynst thy aduersaries.

passages.name: Bagates
passages.head: If thou wilte be victorious agaynst thy aduersaries
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Bagates, & it is of diuerse colors The auncient phylosophers say that it hathe bene proued in the prince Alcides, which how longe he dyd beare it, he had alwayes victory: and it is a stoone of dyuerse coloures, lyke the skynne of a kydde.

passages.name: Bena
passages.head: If thou wilt know before any thyng to come
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Bena, which is lyke a beastes to the, and put it vnder thy tung. And as Aaron and the old Phylosophers sayth, how longe thou wilt holde it so alwayes coniecturing, thou shalt prophecy thinges to come, and thou shalte not erre in any wyse for iudgyng.

passages.name: Histmos
passages.head: If thou wilt know before any thyng to come
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Histmos, which as Isidorus sayeth, is lyke to saffron. And it is founde in a parte of Spayne. Thys stone bloweth like a payre of bellowes, by reason of the wyndinesse in it, it is found nygh the Gades of Hercules, that is twoo Iles, by the further partes of Spayn beyond Garnade, and yf thys stone be set in a garment, it can be burned in no wyse, but it shyneth lyke fyre.
passages.title: If thou wilt that thy garmente be vnable to be burned

passages.name: Tabrices
passages.head: If thou wilt haue fauour and honour
passages.text: Take the stone, whiche is called Tabrices, and it is lyke too the Chrystall stoone. The aunciente Phylosophers, as Euax, and Aaron, saye of it, that it geueth eloquence, fauoure and honoure, and it is sayde moreouer, that it healeth euery dropsye.

passages.name: Chrysolite
passages.head: If thou wilt dryue away fantasies and folishnes
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Chrysolitus, and it is of the same vertue with Attemicus, as Aarom & Euax say, in the boke of the natures of herbes, & stones: this stone set in golde, & borne, dryueth away folishnes, & expelleth fantasies. It is affyrmed to geue wysedome, and it is good against feare.

passages.name: Geratides
passages.head: If thou wilt iudge the opynions and thoughtes of others
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Geratides, & it is of black colour let one holde it in his mouthe, it maketh hym that beareth it mery and in sauour, & well estemed with all men.

passages.name: Radianus
passages.head: If thou woulde optayne anye thinge of any man
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Radianus, & it is blacke, shyning through, which whan the heade of a Cocke is geuen to Emotes, or Pysmeres to eate, it is founde a longe tyme after, in the head of the Cocke. And thesame stone is also called Conatides.

passages.name: Luperius
passages.head: If thou woulde make, that nether dogges, nor hunters maye hurt any beast, which they hunte
passages.text: Put before them the stoone, which is called Luperius, and it will runne soone to the stoone. Thys stone is found in Lybia, & all beastes runne to it, as to their defender. It letteth that neyther dogges, nor hunters maye hurt them.

passages.name: Unces
passages.head: If thou wilt burne any mans hande without fyre
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Unces, which we called before Principem apti, whiche is fyre, & it is as fyre. If any mam strayn hard thys stone, it burneth soone hys hande, lyke as it ware burned with a materiall fyre, whiche is a meruaylous thynge.

passages.name: Lapis lazuli
passages.head: If thou wilt cure melancoly, or a feuer quartaine, in any mam
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Lapis lazuli. It is like to the colour of the heauen, and there is within it little bodyes of golde. And it is sure and proued, that it cureth melancholye, and the feuer quartayne.

passages.name: Emerald
passages.head: If thou wolde make any m… witte sharpe and quicke, and augmente hys ryches, and also prophecy thynges to come
passages.text: It is taken out of the nestes of grypes or grystons, it doth bothe comforte and saue, and beynge borne, it maketh a man to vnderstande well, and geueth to hym a good memory, augmenteth the ryches of hym that beareth it, & yf any man shall holde it vnder hys tung, he shall prophecy anone.

passages.name: Iris
passages.head: If thou wilt make a rayne bowe to appeare
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Iris, & it is whyte lyke the Cristall, four square or hauinge hornes. If thys stone be put in the beame of the Sunne, by turning backe it maketh a rayne bowe soone to appere in the walle.

passages.name: Gallasia
passages.head: If thou wilt make a stone, whych maye neuer be made hote
passages.text: Take the stone which is called Gallasia it hath the figure of hayl. & the colour and hardnesse of the Dyamonde, If this stone be put in a very great fyre, it will neuer be hote. And the cause is, for it hath the holes so strat together, that the heate may not enter in the body of the stone. Also Aaron & Euax say, that this stone borne mitigateth, wrathe, lecherye and other hote passions.

passages.name: Draconites
passages.head: If thou wilte ouercome thy enemyes
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called …raconites, from the Dragons head, and yf the stone be drawen out from hym alyue, it is good agaynste all poysons, and he that beareth it in hys lefte arme, shal ouercome all hys enemyes.

passages.name: Tepistites
passages.head: If thou wilt make a mam sure
passages.text: Take the stone which is called Tepistites. It is founde in the sea it is shyninge & ruddy. And it is sayde in the boke of Alchorath, that if it be borne before the harte, it maketh a man sure, & refraineth & mitigateth all seditions, & discordes. It is sayd also, that it mitigateth the flyes, with long hynder legges, which bourneth corn with touching of it, & deuoureth the residew, soules, cloudes, hayle, and such as haue power of the fruites of the earth. And it hath ben proued of philophers of lat time and of certayn of oure brethren, that it being put against the beam of the sunne putteth furth fiery beames. Also yf this stone be put in seething water, the seethinge will soone cease, and the water wilbe colde a litle after.

passages.name: Jacinth
passages.head: If thou wilt that straungers walke sure and safe
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Hyacinthus, in English a Jacinct, it is of many colours. The grene is best, & it hath reade vaynes, & should be set in syluer, and it is said in certain lectures, that ther is two kyndes of it, of the water, & of the Saphyre. The Jacinct of the water, is yelow, whyte The iacinct of the Saphyrs, is very shyning yelowe, hauing no watrishnesse, & this is better, & it is written of thys, in lecturs of philosophers, that it beyng borne on the fynger, or necke, maketh straungers sure, & acceptable, to theyr ghestes. And it prouoketh sleape, for the coldnesse of it, & the Jacinct of Saphyre hath properly thys.

passages.name: Orithes
passages.head: If thou wilt be saued from diuers chaunces and pestilent bittes
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called Orithes, of whiche there be.iii. kindes, one black, an other grene and the thyrde, of the which, one parte is roughe, and the other playn, and the colour of it is like the colour of plate of yron, but the grene hath whyte spottes. Thys stone borne, preserueth from dyuerse chaunces, and perilles of death.

passages.name: Sapphire
passages.head: If thou wilt make peace
passages.text: Take the stone, which is called a Saphyre, whiche commeth from the Easte vnto Inde, & it that is of yelowe coloure is best, whyche is not verye brighte, it maketh peace and concorde, it maketh the myndepure and deuote toward God, it strengtheneth the mynde in good thynges, & maketh a mam to cole from inwarde heate.

passages.name: Owl
passages.head: The thyrde boke of Albertus Magnus, of the vertues of certayn beastes
passages.text: Bubo, a shricke owle, is a byrd well ynough knowen, whiche is called Magis of the Chaldeis, & Hysopus of the Greekes. There be meruaylous vertues of thys fowle, for yf the hart and righte foote of it, be putte vpon a man sleapyng, he shall say anone to the whatsoeuer thou shalte aske of hym. And thys hath ben proued a late tyme of our brethren. And yf any man put thys vnder hys arme hole, no dogge will barke at hym, but kepe silence. And yf these thinges aforesayde, ioyned together with a wynge of it, he hanged vp to a tree, byrdes wyll gather together to that tree.

passages.name: Camel
passages.head: The thyrde boke of Albertus Magnus, of the vertues of certayn beastes
passages.text: Camelus, the Camel is a beast knowen well ynough. It is called of the Chaldeis Ciboi, of the Grekes Iphim. If the bloude of it be put into the skyn of the beast called Stellio, & then set on any mans head, which is lyke a lysard, hauing on his backe spottes like stetres, it shall seme that he is a gyant, & that hys head is in heauen. And thys is sayd in the boke of Alchorath, of Mercury, And yf a lantern anointed with the bloud of it, be lyghtenned, it shall … that all men standynge aboute haue Camelles headdes, so that there be no outward light of an other candeil.

passages.name: Hare
passages.head: The thyrde boke of Albertus Magnus, of the vertues of certayn beastes
passages.text: Lepus, the hare is a beast wel ynough knowen, of the Chaldeis it is called Ueterellum, and of the Grekes Onollosa, the vertue of it is shewed to be merualous, for Euax and Aaron sayd that the, fete of it ioyned with a stone or with the head of a blacke owsell, moueth a man to hardines, so that he feare not death.

passages.name: Lion
passages.head: The thyrde boke of Albertus Magnus, of the vertues of certayn beastes
passages.text: Leo, a Lyon is a beaste well ynough knowen, of the Chaldeis called Balamus, of the Greekes Beruth. If thonges of lether be made of the skynne of hym, & a man gyrded with theym, he shall not feare hys enemies. And yf any man will eate of the flesh of hym, & will drynke of hys water for thre dayes, he shall be cured from the feuer quartaine. And if any parte of hys eyes be put vnder a mans arme hole & borne, al beastes shall flee away, bowynge doune their hade vnto their low belyes.

passages.name: Porpoise
passages.head: The thyrde boke of Albertus Magnus, of the vertues of certayn beastes
passages.text: Foca, purpays is a fysh well ynough knowen, of the Chaldeis it is called Daulaubur, of the grecians Labor, this fysh is of diuers nature. If the tung of it be takem, and be put with a litle of the harte of it in water, for a suerty fyshes will gather there together. And yf thou wilte beare it vnder thy arme hole, no man shalbe able to haue victorye againste the, thou shalt haue a gentle & pleasaunte iudge.

passages.name: Eel
passages.head: The thyrde boke of Albertus Magnus, of the vertues of certayn beastes
passages.text: Auguilla, an eele, it is a fysshe sufficiently knowem. The vertues of it are meruaylous, as Euar & Aaron saye, for if it dye for fault of water, the harte remaynynge hole, and strong vyneger to takem and it be myxed to the bloude of the fowle, called in Latine Uultur, which some call in English a Grype, and some a rauyn, and be put vnder dunge in any place, thei shall all how many soeuer they be, recouer their lyfe, as they had before. And if the worme of thys eele be drawen out, and put in the aforesayd confection, the space of one moneth, the worme shalbe chaunged into a very blacke eele of whiche, if any man shall eate, he shall dye.

passages.name: Hoopoe
passages.head: The thyrde boke of Albertus Magnus, of the vertues of certayn beastes
passages.text: Upupa, the Lapwynke or blacke plouer, is a byrd sufficiently knowen, of the Chaldeis it is called Boridicta, of the Grekes I son, the eyes of it born, make a mam grosse or great. And if the eyes of it be borne before a mans breast, all his enemies shalbe pacefied. And yf thou shalt haue the heade of it in thy purse, thou canst not be deceiued of any merchaunt. Thys hath ben proued this daye of our brethren.

passages.name: Pelican
passages.head: The thyrde boke of Albertus Magnus, of the vertues of certayn beastes
passages.text: Pellicianus, the Pellicane is a byrd sufficiently knowen, it is called of the Chaldeis Uoltri, & of the Grekes Iphalari. The vertue of it is meruaylous. If yonge byrdes be kylled and their harte not be broken, & if a parte of her bloud be taken and be put warme in the mouth of the yonge byrdes, they wil receyue soone agayn lyfe as before.

passages.name: Raven
passages.head: The thyrde boke of Albertus Magnus, of the vertues of certayn beastes
passages.text: Coruus, called of some a rauem, and of others a crow, the vertue of thys fowle is meruaylous, as Euax and Aaron reherse. If her egges be sodden, & be put agayne in the nest, the rauen goeth sone to the read sea, in a certayne Ile where Aldoricus or Alodrius is buryed, and she bryngeth a stone where with she toucheth her egges, and the egges be soone rawe as they ware before. It is a meruaylous thynge to styrre vp sodden egges. If thys stoone be put in a rynge, & the leaf of the laurel tree put vnder it, & a man beyng bounden in chaynes, or a doore shutte, be toucheth therwith, he that is boundem shall sone be lowsed, and the doore shalbe opened. And yf this stone be put in a mans mouth, it geueth too hym vnderstanding of all byrdes. The stone is of Inde, because it is founde in Inde, after certayn wyse men, & sometyme in the read sea. It is of diuerse colours, & it maketh a man to forgete all wrathe, as we haue said aboue in the same stone

passages.name: Mole
passages.head: The thyrde boke of Albertus Magnus, of the vertues of certayn beastes
passages.text: Talpa, a molle is a beast well ynough knowen. The vertue of thys beast is meruaylous, as it is rehearsed of Phylosophers. If the fore of it be wrapped in the leaf of a Laurell tree, & be put in the mouth of an horse, he wil flee for feare. And if it be put in the neste of any fowle, there shal neuer come forth yong byrdes of these egges.

passages.name: Blackbird
passages.head: The thyrde boke of Albertus Magnus, of the vertues of certayn beastes
passages.text: Merula, a blacke macke or ow sell, is a fowle well ynough knowen, and the vertue of it is mernaylous. For if the fethers of the righte wynge of it be hanged vp in the myddes of an house, with a read leafe, which was neuer occupyed, no man shalbe able too s…epe in that house, vntyll it be put awaye. And yf the harte of it be put vnder the heade of a man slepyng, & he be inquired, he will saye all that he hath done wyth an hye voyce.

passages.name: Dog
passages.head: The thyrde boke of Albertus Magnus, of the vertues of certayn beastes
passages.text: If anye man beare a dogges hart on his left syde, all that dogges shall holde their peace, and not barke at hym.

passages.name: Wolf
passages.head: The thyrde boke of Albertus Magnus, of the vertues of certayn beastes
passages.text: If any man will bynd that right eye of an Wolfe on his right sleue neyther men nor dogges maye hurte hym.

passages.name: Palm tree
passages.head: Here beginneth the boke of the meruayles of the world, set forth by Albertus Magnus
passages.text: Therfore the lode stone draweth yron to it, and a certayne other stone draweth glasse. So meruaylous thinges are declared of phylosophers to be in thinges by experience, whyche no man ought to denye. And that is not proued after the fashion of philosophers whych founde that, for the phylosophers saith, that the palme is a tree, and it hath the male and the female, therfore whan the female is nygh the male, thou seest that the female, bowe doune to the male, and the leafe & braunches of it are made softe, and bowe doune to the male.

passages.name: Cockatrice
passages.head: Here beginneth the boke of the meruayles of the world, set forth by Albertus Magnus
passages.text: And in the boke De cyriaca of Galene, it is sayde that the Serpent which is called Regulus in Latin, a cokatryce in Englishe, is some what whyte, vpom whose head there be thre hayres, & wham any mam seeth them he dieth sone And whan any mam or any other lyuing thing heareth his whiste lynge, he dyeth. And euery beaste that eateth. of it beinge deade, dieth also. And aristotel sayde, where there is sommer.vi. Monethes and lykewise winter, there is a floud in the which adders are founde, whose property is, that they neuer se them selues but they dye, but whan they be dead, they hurt not. And aristotele put craftly in the mind of Alexander, that he shoulde take a greate glasse, and walke wyth it towarde them, & whan they dyd beholde them selues in the glasse they dyed. This sayng of Aristotel was not beleued of some men For Auicenna sayd agaynst Aristotel, yf any man dyd see it, he dyed, wherefore there is no truthe in his speache.

passages.name: Beast
passages.head: Here beginneth the boke of the meruayles of the world, set forth by Albertus Magnus
passages.text: And Philosophers saye, whan thou wilt that a beast returne to hys lodging, anoint his forehead with Sepesquilla, and it wil returne.

passages.name: Calf
passages.head: Here beginneth the boke of the meruayles of the world, set forth by Albertus Magnus
passages.text: And Aristotel sayd in the boke of the beastes. If any mam put wrought wax vpon the hornes of cowes calfe, it wil goo with hym whersoeuer he wil wtout labour And if any man anointe the horne of kye with waxe and oile or pitche the payne of their fete goeth away.

passages.name: Cock
passages.head: Here beginneth the boke of the meruayles of the world, set forth by Albertus Magnus
passages.text: if thou desire that a cocke …rowe not, anoynte his head & fore heade with oyle.

passages.name: Ant
passages.head: Here beginneth the boke of the meruayles of the world, set forth by Albertus Magnus
passages.text: And if the dunge of an hare be broken vnto poulder and caste abrode vpon a place of Emotes or Pismeres, than the Pismeres leaue there place.

passages.name: Sponge
passages.head: Here beginneth the boke of the meruayles of the world, set forth by Albertus Magnus
passages.text: And it is sayde that when a sponge is caste in wyne mixed with water and after drawen forthe & strayned and wrynged, the water commeth sorth of it, & the wyne remayneth, yf it be not mixed, nothynge commeth forth.

passages.name: Ass
passages.head: Here beginneth the boke of the meruayles of the world, set forth by Albertus Magnus
passages.text: It is sayde also, that yf anye stone be bounden to the tayle of an asse, he wil not bray nor rore.

passages.name: Eagle
passages.head: Here beginneth the boke of the meruayles of the world, set forth by Albertus Magnus
passages.text: And philosphers sayde that whan the fethers of Eagles be put with the fethers of other fowles, they burne and mortefye them for as he ouercometh in hys lyfe all byrds, & hath rule ouer them so the fethers of Eagles are deadly to all fethers.

passages.name: Ass
passages.head: Here beginneth the boke of the meruayles of the world, set forth by Albertus Magnus
passages.text: And yf thou parfume an house or place with the lunges or lightes of an Asse, thou clengest it from euery Serpente and Scorpion. And of thys Philosophers know that it is good agaynst poyson.

passages.name: Mule
passages.head: Here beginneth the boke of the meruayles of the world, set forth by Albertus Magnus
passages.text: And whan the house is perfumed with the lefte houfe of a mule, flyes remayne not in it.

passages.name: Horse
passages.head: Here beginneth the boke of the meruayles of the world, set forth by Albertus Magnus
passages.text: A grosse and styffe hayre of a mares tayll, put vppon a doore suffereth not zauzales to enter.

passages.name: Glow-worm
passages.head: Here beginneth the boke of the meruayles of the world, set forth by Albertus Magnus
passages.text: To write letters or bils, which be not readde but in the nyghte, take the gall of a snayle or mylk of a so we, and put it too the fyre, or with water of a worme shynyng late.

passages.name: Topaz
passages.head: Here beginneth the boke of the meruayles of the world, set forth by Albertus Magnus
passages.text: If ye myngell together many whites of hennes egges, a moneth after they are made glasse, & hard as a stoone, and of thys beynge after thys fasshion is mayde a Sophisticall precious stone, called Topasius, yf it bee conioyned before wyth Saffron or read earthe.

passages.name: Eel
passages.head: Here beginneth the boke of the meruayles of the world, set forth by Albertus Magnus
passages.text: And yf any manne shall haue many eeles in a wyne vessell, and they be suffered to dye in it, if any man drynke of it, he shal abhorre wyne for a yeare, and by chaunce euermore.

passages.name: Hangman's rope
passages.head: Here beginneth the boke of the meruayles of the world, set forth by Albertus Magnus
passages.text: And it is sayde, yf a rope be taken, with whyche a theefe is or hath ben hanged vp with, and a litle chaffe, which a whyrle wind lifted vp in the ayre, and let them be put in a potte, and set among other pottes, that pot shal breake all the other pottes.

passages.name: Hangman's rope
passages.head: Here beginneth the boke of the meruayles of the world, set forth by Albertus Magnus
passages.text: Also take thou a litle of the aforesayd rope, and put it on the instrument, with which the breade is put in the ouen, whan he that shoulde put it in the ouen, should put it in, he shall not be able too put it in, but it shall leape out.

passages.name: Lamp
passages.head: That men maye seme without heades
passages.text: Take the fatte out of the eare of a dogge, anoynte with it a litle newe sylke, put it in a new lampe of greene glasse, and put the lampe amonge men, & they shall see the vysage of a dogge.
passages.title: That men maye seme to haue the visage or countenaunce of a dogge

passages.name: Rope
passages.head: That men maye seme without heades
passages.text: Take of the hayr of a dead asse, and make a rope, & drye it, & take the mary of the principall bone of hys ryght shoulder, and myxe it with virgyns waxe, & anoynte the corde, and put it vpon the thras sholdes of the house, they that come into the house shall seme to haue thre headdes, and they that be in the house shall seme Asses to them that enter in.
passages.title: That men maye seme to haue thre headdes

passages.name: Ass
passages.head: That men maye seme without heades
passages.text: Take vp of the couering of an Asse & anoynte the mam on his head.
passages.title: If thou wilt that a mans head seme an Asse head

passages.name: Birds
passages.head: If thou wilte vnderstande the voyces of byrdes
passages.text: Associate with the two felows in the.xxviii. daye of October, & go in to a certayne woode wyth dogges as too hunte, and carye home wyth that beaste, whyche thou shalt fynd first, and prepare it with the harte of a Foxe, and thou shalt vnderstand anone the voyce of byrdes or beastes. And if thou wilte that any other lykewise vnderstande, kysse hym, and he shall vnderstande.

passages.name: Magpie
passages.head: If thou wilt louse bondes
passages.text: Go into the woode, and loke where the Pye hath her nest with her byrdes, and whan thou shalt be there, clymme vp the tree, and bynde about the hole of it whersoeuer thou wilt. For whan she seeth the, she goeth for a certayn herbe, whiche she will put to the binding, and it is broken anone, and that herbe falleth to the ground vpom the cloth, which thou should haue put vnder the tree, and be the present, and take it.

passages.name: Dream
passages.head: If thou wilt louse bondes
passages.text: Take the bloude of an Asse congeled, and the fatte Lupi cerini, and a swete incense or gumme called Storax and also Storax, & also styrax, gather it altogether by equall weyghtes, and let them be mixed, and graynes or cornes be made therof, and let the house be perfumed with them, than thou shalt se hym in thy sleape, that shall shewe to the all thynges.
passages.title: A perfumynge too see in oure s…eape what thing is to come of good and euell

passages.name: Candle
passages.head: If thou wilt louse bondes
passages.text: Take the eyes of an shriche owle, the eyes of a fyshe, which is called Affures, and the eyes of a fyshe, whiche is called Libinitis, and the galle of wolfes, breake theym with thy handes, & myxe them together, and put them in a vessell of glasse, than whan thou wilt warke it, take the fatte of any beast thou wilt, that this may be made in the shape of it, melte it, and myxe it perfitely with that medicine, and anoynte the matche or candel weke, whatsoeuer thou wilt with it. After kendle it in the middes of the house, and the mem shall seme in the shape of that beaste, whose fatte thou did take.
passages.title: A maner of makyng a matche of a candell, or candel weke, which whan thou shalt kendle, thou shalte see men, in what shape soeuer thou wilt

passages.name: Candle
passages.head: If thou wilt louse bondes
passages.text: Take the eyes of a fyshe, & the eyes of Filoe, that is of a breaker of bones, and breake them with thy handes, and make them soft, and put them in a vessell of glasse vii. dayes After put some oyle in them, and lyghten it in a greene lampe, and put it before menne, whiche be in the house, they shal see them selfes in the shape of aum gels by the lyght of the fyre.
passages.title: An other matche of a candell or a candell weke, that men may appere in the shape of aungels

passages.name: Lamp
passages.head: If thou wilt louse bondes
passages.text: Take the bloude of a snayl, drye it vp in a linen cloth, & make of it a weke, and lyghten it in a lampe, geue it to any man thou wilt, & saye lighten thys, he shall not cease to farte, vntyll he let it departe, and it is a meruaylous thynge.
passages.title: A meruaylous operation of a lampe, whiche yf anye man shall holde, he ceaseth not to farte, vntyll he shall leaue it

passages.name: Lamp
passages.head: If thou wilt louse bondes
passages.text: Take a spice, which is called Spuma, after bray it, and after make it with water of Camphere, and anoynte thy handes with it, after open them in the mouth of the lampe, the lyghte of it shalbe put out, and close them, & it shalbe kendled agayne.
passages.title: If thou wilt make that whan thou openest thy handes vpon a lampe, the light of it is put out, and whan thou closest them vpom it, it kendled, and it ceaseth not to do that
